What runs where, and in which language

Top

Three questions decide whether a library fits your constraint, and the answers are measured against the code rather than claimed. They are stated here once so you do not have to read seventeen READMEs to find them.

Local and free, or paid cloud

Sixteen of the seventeen never contact a paid service. They run on your machine with open-source tooling: no account, no API key, no per-character or per-token billing. Where a model is involved the weights download once, then the work is offline.

Two of them do reach a remote server, and the distinction matters: bucket-helper and sftp-helper talk to storage and servers that are yours — an S3 bucket, a host you have an account on. That is your infrastructure, not a third-party tariff; their whole job is moving data to a place you chose.

best-engine-ai-helper is the only one that can call a paid cloud, and only when you ask it to. Its default path is the local model. A cloud provider is reached only if you name an engine that declares an api_key_env field and set that environment variable; the key is read from the environment at call time and never written to disk. So the paid path exists, it is opt-in, and it is one explicit gesture away — never a default that bills you by surprise.

Offline, or real time

Batch and streaming are different objectives, not settings on a dial. Offline work has no deadline, so quality is the only thing to maximise. Real-time work has a hard feasibility boundary: the engine must produce faster than playback consumes, which is a real-time factor below 1 — and below about 0.8 once you leave margin for the first chunk and for jitter.

The libraries that genuinely stream, verified by the shape of their public API rather than by their prose: capture-helper (iter_camera_frames, iter_mic_audio), podcast-helper (extract_audio_stream), video-helper (extract_frames, iter_frame_optical_flow), speaker-helper (Speaker.stream) and vocal-helper (Pipeline.run, live, beside an OfflinePipeline that is explicitly the batch twin). discussion-helper is real-time by construction — it is a conversation loop — and it drives those two rather than streaming itself.

speaker-helper is where the two objectives visibly diverge, and its router picks by condition instead of pretending one engine wins both. For streaming it chooses kokoro, the only engine whose real-time factor is measured under the ceiling: the router refuses to claim an engine keeps up if it was never timed. The two halves of that choice come from different places, and the router records which: speed is timed on your machine, while quality is ranked by a public_elo — a human-preference arena score measured elsewhere, by other people, because preference is not something a laptop can measure. For offline, where speed is disregarded entirely, it chooses kyutai in French and chatterbox in English, ranked on the engine prior rather than on an arena. Everything else in the suite is batch, which is not a limitation but the honest shape of converting a file.

Languages

Most of the suite is language-agnostic: resampling a WAV, compressing a video or hashing a folder does not care what language is in the file. Language becomes a real parameter only where meaning is involved, and there the libraries say which ones they cover rather than implying all of them.

vocal-helper identifies the language it hears and transcribes it; speaker-helper ships female default voices per language and routes per language, with French and English as the measured pair and a multilingual engine behind the others; discussion-helper inherits both. md2star localises the documents it produces — the bibliography heading follows the document's own language. standpoint writes its analysis in French or English. Everything user-facing across the suite exists in both languages, which is why every page here has a French twin.

os-helper

Audio & Voice

Top

audio-helper

Load, convert, split and concatenate audio; optional source separation.

📃 Docs · 📦 PyPI · 🐙 GitHub

vocal-helper

Live PCM → Voice Activity Detection → online speaker diarization → Speech to Text → optional LLM summary.

📃 Docs · 📦 PyPI · 🐙 GitHub

speaker-helper

Speech synthesis in your own process: say a sentence, stream a reply, or narrate a document with the timed track that lets a page follow along. Every engine is local and free — no API key, no per-character billing, offline once the weights land. The router picks by condition: streaming favours speed (kokoro, RTF under 0.8), offline favours quality (kyutai for French, chatterbox for English). A pronunciation lexicon states once how a word is said. The inverse of vocal-helper: text in, speech out.

📃 Docs · 📦 PyPI · 🐙 GitHub

discussion-helper

Hold a spoken conversation at the microphone: listen, answer, speak — and stop the moment the user cuts in. The loop that knows whose turn it is.

📃 Docs · 📦 PyPI · 🐙 GitHub
